articles.title_orig: Everything you need to know about Black Friday 2026, according to our deals expert | CNN Underscored
articles.title_zh: Everything you need to know about Black Friday 2026, according to our deals expert | CNN Underscored
articles.content_orig:
If you buy something through a link in this article, we may earn commission.
Halloween is in the rearview mirror. Next stop: Black Friday sales, which have started earlier than ever, creeping in the first week of November and lasting the entire month. That's good news for those of you who hemmed and hawed on a big tech buy during Prime Day in October. You still have time to score best-of-the-year pricing from Beats, Bose, Amazon, Apple and nearly every other major brand, plus plenty of minor ones.
Instead of waiting until my post-turkey nap, I rounded up the best tech deals now. That way you're not refreshing deal pages at the Thanksgiving table. Better yet, buy those headphones you've had your eye on now and you can just sit back and enjoy some noise-cancelling silence on the flight to see family.
AirPods Pro 3 ($199, was $249) Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus ($40, was $70) Apple iPad 11-inch (A16) ($399, was $449) Ring Battery Doorbell 2K ($40, was $99) Apple AirTags (2nd Gen) 4-pack ($80, was $99)
Black Friday always falls on the day after Thanksgiving, which this year is Friday, Nov. 27. It used to be a one-day event, but these days, anyone calling it a single-day sale is either lying or completely out of touch. Most major retailers will roll out discounts weeks in advance — think of it as "Black November." That means you'll want to start keeping tabs on prices now, and who knows? You might be done with all of your holiday shopping before the turkey coma hits.
Not necessarily everything , but pretty dang close. We're already seeing close to record-low prices on TVs, laptops and headphones, and it's common to see gaming consoles and appliances go on sale too.
Pretty much. The usual suspects — Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Macy's, Kohl's, Wayfair, The Home Depot — will all go big. Smaller brands often join in too, though some do it quietly (think: an unadvertised 20% off code hidden at checkout). Others, like REI, make a point to not have a sale with the rest of them, instead opting for earlier sales. The point is, if you're shopping online at all this fall, there's no excuse to pay full price.
Have a plan (or even better, a spreadsheet): Ever end up overspending while grocery shopping when you don't have a list? Me too. Don't wait until the week of Thanksgiving (or later) to decide what to buy. Create a wishlist and track prices starting now. Once that dream TV, laptop or pair of noise-cancelling headphones drops to a real all-time low, jump on it — good deals don't linger.
Do your homework: Don't rely on a single retailer. In most cases, it pays to shop around. Prices also tend to fluctuate, so don't assume the first small markdown you see is the best one.
Be skeptical: Here's a dirty little secret: Some "sales" aren't really sales. Retailers bump prices before big events so the discount looks steeper. Web tools like Honey or CamelCamelCamel can show you price history (to see if that 95% off gadget has ever sold at MSRP), but if you don't feel like going full spreadsheet mode, I'll be doing that work for you all month long — rounding up legit deals, not the fake ones.

articles.title_orig: King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row
articles.title_zh: King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row
articles.content_orig:
The King's role as head of the Commonwealth is about "inspiring and convening, rather than policy making", says Buckingham Palace - distancing him from rows over whether the UK should apologise and make reparations for its part in the Atlantic slave trade.
The Palace statement clarifying the King's non-political role in the Commonwealth comes as the organisation's leaders gather for a summit in Antigua and Barbuda.
The King is to deliver a speech on Tuesday which is expected to recognise the painful legacy of slavery. But his speech will reflect the position of the UK government.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had suggested there could be some form of apology over slavery, but has ruled out financial reparations.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
On Saturday, the prime minister said that the UK "must face up to the past" over the "brutal and barbaric violation" of the slave trade, and that he was "open" to the possibility of a formal apology.
But on Monday, his official spokesperson said that while Burnham had "expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade", this was "distinct from a formal apology".
Burnham thought it was "right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected", his spokesperson said.
"An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected," they added.
Meanwhile Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK was "self-confident enough to have this conversation".
"The dialogue we're setting up will consider whether and how a formal apology could help acknowledge the history, help heal the division and support stronger relationships for the future," Miliband said.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has rejected "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving the UK's current problems.
Gaston Brown, Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda, the country which is hosting the Commonwealth gathering, says that the consequences of slavery "have not disappeared with the passage of time" and wants to discuss reparations.
Whichever way the King's speech addresses the subject of slavery will be a political decision.
On previous occasions, the King has used strong language, such as talking about his "greatest sorrow and regret" at the "abhorrent and unjustifiable acts of violence" of the colonial era on a visit to Kenya.
And in Antigua he is expected to voice his "sincere sorrow", having spoken about the "great suffering of the past" in the Bahamas last week.
But any formal apology and any action on reparations on behalf of the UK would be a decision for political leaders - and the statement from the Palace defuses any expectation of such an intervention.
Instead the Palace sets out the King's role as a unifying figure above such divisions, with the Commonwealth described as a "family" of nations.
The King's "most significant contribution has been helping to connect leaders, institutions and investors - many of whom he knows personally from his many years of international diplomacy", says the Palace.
And that relates to "shared areas of interest and concern, creating the conditions in which ambitious Commonwealth-led initiatives can emerge and succeed".
It's a view of a positive and collective approach of the King's role in the Commonwealth, bringing together politicians with business leaders, philanthropists and civil society.
The King is on a tour of the Caribbean and touched down in Antigua and Barbuda on Friday, having visited the Bahamas and Guyana.
On Monday, along with Queen Camilla, he toured the museum at Antigua's Government House where they viewed slavery artefacts including shackles and diagrams of ships packed with enslaved people.
He also encountered actor Idris Elba during a separate visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base which is now a tourist attraction in the south-east of Antigua.
The Luther actor, who is a goodwill ambassador for the King's Trust, was at the site to host a concert as part of the Commonwealth summit.
Monday also saw Burnham arrive in the country's capital of Saint John's, accompanied by his wife, ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: China Is Sending AI-Powered Robots Into the Ocean to Uncover Its Lost Ancient History
articles.title_zh: China Is Sending AI-Powered Robots Into the Ocean to Uncover Its Lost Ancient History
articles.content_orig:
China's next five-year archaeological plan, covering 2026 to 2030 , proposes deploying artificial intelligence, ancient-DNA analysis, remote sensing and deep-sea robots across some of the country's most significant historical sites. The program is designed to recover artifacts, reconstruct damaged objects and investigate questions about human migration, early states and maritime trade that conventional excavation has so far left only partially answered.
Excavations routinely produce large quantities of broken, scattered material whose connections are difficult to establish manually. Specialized AI systems would identify artifact fragments, match pieces to one another and generate virtual restorations , allowing researchers to study an object's probable original appearance without physically altering the surviving material.
Each pillar of the plan addresses a distinct limitation of conventional archaeological methods.
Remote sensing , which uses aerial or satellite data to detect buried structures, could help researchers locate remains before excavation begins. Ancient-DNA analysis would contribute to population research, tracing relationships, migrations and environmental adaptation among communities that lived thousands of years ago. Usable results require biological material preserved well enough to avoid contamination.
Underwater robotics addresses sites that human divers cannot safely reach. The plan calls for purpose-built deep-sea robots , specialized diving equipment and precision excavation tools aimed at shipwrecks and Maritime Silk Road routes lying on the seabed.
Institutionally, the program is intended to be permanent rather than a series of isolated projects. The official plan describes a national-level archaeological laboratory and a maritime-archaeology hub in Qingdao, signaling an effort to embed high-technology research into standing infrastructure.
Named sites and international partnerships give the blueprint a concrete geographic scope.
Research targets extend from northern China's earliest known sites through the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and across Eurasia. Among the domestic priorities is the transition from Paleolithic hunter-gatherer life to agriculture and settled communities along the Yellow River, Yangtze River and southern Lingnan region.
Major Bronze Age and early-state sites, including Sanxingdui , Erlitou and Yinxu, feature prominently alongside historical infrastructure such as the Qin dynasty Direct Road, the Great Wall and the Grand Canal. International partnerships with institutions in Egypt, Greece, Saudi Arabia and Tunisia are planned for comparative research, underwater surveys and heritage preservation.
The Nanhai No. 1 shows what underwater excavation can recover and what it demands in return.
The Nanhai No. 1 , a Southern Song-era merchant vessel associated with trade between China and overseas markets, illustrates why underwater archaeology occupies a central place in the new blueprint. Discovered in 1987 and raised intact in 2007, the wreck was transferred to a purpose-built aquatic environment at the Guangdong Maritime Silk Road Museum, where conservation and excavation continue under controlled conditions.
UNESCO describes the site as unusually valuable because its preservation captures cargo and food remains that document commerce and daily life aboard the vessel. According to a government-linked report, more than 180,000 cultural relics have been salvaged and preserved from the site.
Ambition and evidence are not the same thing, and the plan's limits deserve equal billing.
AI cannot reconstruct information the surviving evidence does not support; a virtual restoration is only as reliable as the fragments behind it. Deep-sea robots still contend with pressure, poor visibility, currents and fragile materials.
Ancient-DNA results depend on preservation conditions and rigorous contamination controls, and their interpretation requires care. None of this invalidates the program's potential, but discovery and conclusion are not the same thing.
The blueprint's stated cultural objectives are as significant as its scientific ones, and they invite scrutiny.
The plan carries an explicit cultural objective alongside its scientific aims: increasing China's international influence over interpretations of its history and civilization. That goal raises practical questions about data access, interpretive independence and the terms under which foreign institutions will participate. How those questions are answered will determine whether the international partnerships function as genuine scholarly collaboration or primarily serve a national framing agenda. Those details remain unclear and will merit close attention as the program moves from blueprint to fieldwork.

articles.title_orig: Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push
articles.title_zh: Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push
articles.content_orig:
China sales fell 31% last quarter, yet Mercedes says it is “indispensable” and plans to build future Chinese-market cars almost entirely with local parts.
2027 Mercedes-Benz CLA 220 Hybrid in Manufaktur Patagonia Red
Mercedes-Benz , though currently struggling to retain market position in China, says it will give a broader 2030 strategy update, which will include a detailed review of its China business, next year. The numbers explain the urgency: German brands have been getting crushed in China .
Mercedes-Benz is doubling down on the market that is hurting it most. According to Reuters , CEO Ola Källenius calls China an “indispensable market and innovation hub.
Third-quarter Mercedes-Benz Cars sales fell 8 percent to 407,232, with China down 31 percent to 86,800, according to BigGo . Elsewhere, Europe was up 5 percent, Germany was up 13 percent, and the US was up 6 percent, with record battery-electric sales up 61 percent. Adjusted return on sales for cars dropped to 2.5 percent from 4.8 percent, and Mercedes cut its full-year guidance to 2-3 percent from 3-5 percent; its CFO called the fourth quarter “a break-even quarter.”
Starting with the electric E-Class in the second half of 2027, Källenius said Mercedes will source “almost everything” in China for Chinese production. According to reports, CFO Harald Wilhelm also wants the company to rely less on China as a profit source. That is a split-screen strategy: stay in the world’s largest car market, but with local suppliers and less exposure to its price war. Mercedes has already felt that pain from tariffs and China’s EV boom.
If you live in the US, this is the good-news part. The China sourcing applies to cars built for China, and nothing in the reporting says it changes what’s sold here. What matters more is where Mercedes is growing: US sales rose 6 percent last quarter, and Källenius said the company plans further US investments and sees potential to lift annual sales from more than 300,000 vehicles toward 400,000, per Reuters. Audi announced a $4 billion US assembly plant that will create around 4,500 jobs. Mercedes too is changing gears in a push for higher volume after years of sliding sales. For buyers, that could mean more attention and more incentives, though nothing has been promised.
In Germany, Mercedes will relaunch a voluntary severance program for indirect staff from December. It booked about €1.8 billion (about $2 billion) in provisions for the last round in 2025, with most of the new program’s earnings impact expected in 2027. Källenius said further German investment depends on productivity and costs, noting US labor costs run at roughly 80 percent of German levels.

articles.title_orig: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.title_zh: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.content_orig:
By GREG HEFFER, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 05:26 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 12:45 EDT, 2 November 2026
Labour today scrapped 11 power-sharing arrangements with the Greens across local councils amid a furious anti-Semitism row.
In the wake of Green members passing a 'Zionism is racism' motion at their conference last month, Labour has ceased cooperation in a slew of local authorities.
Labour officials announced on Monday that the party had ended deals with the Greens in Arun, Derbyshire Dales, Havant, Lewes, Runnymede, Sheffield, Stafford, Warwick, Wealden, West Devon, and West Suffolk.
But Labour will still work with the Greens, who are led nationally by Zack Polanski , on six other councils after local Green groups met the party's conditions for continued cooperation.
It comes after all Labour council groups in coalition or other power-sharing arrangements with the Greens were told to seek 'reassurances' their local partners condemned the 'Zionism is racism' motion.
They were also urged to get confirmation that local Green groups would call on their party's national leadership to rethink the motion.
Labour said the ultimatum impacted a total of 17 councils across England and one in Wales.
The responses were reviewed by Labour's ruling National Executive Committee, with local Labour groups now given 14 days to abide by the body's decisions.
Zack Polanski's poll rating has slumped to his worst as Green leader amid the anti-Semitism row
Andy Burnham has ruled out any coalition with the Greens on a national level in future while the policy declaring Zionism a form of racism is in place
Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said: 'Any local power-sharing arrangement cannot come at the expense of upholding the moral obligation we have to stand up for everyone in our communities and the values we share.
Arun District Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
Broadland District Council : Conditions met – local cooperation to continue.
Coventry City Council : No formal arrangement in place. Conditions not met – no formal arrangement will be made in future.
Derbyshire Dales District Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
Havant Borough Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
Lewes District Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation has been withdrawn.
Monmouthshire County Council : Conditions met – local cooperation to continue.
North Somerset Council : Conditions met – local cooperation to continue.
Rother District Council : Conditions met – local cooperation to continue.
Runnymede Borough Council : Local cooperation has already ceased.
Sheffield City Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation has been withdrawn.
Stafford Borough Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
Warwick District Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
Wealden District Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
West Devon Borough Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
West Oxfordshire District Council : Conditions met – local cooperation to continue.
West Suffolk Council : Conditions not met – local cooperation to be withdrawn.
West Sussex County Council : Conditions met – local cooperation to continue.
Mayor of the West of England Deputy Mayor represents the Green Party. Conditions met – local cooperation to continue.
'Labour has been clear from the start that the 'Zionism is racism' policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government.
'We are pleased that some local Green Parties have rightly opted to disavow this policy and have called on their party's leadership to do the same.
'It is disappointing that some local Green Parties have not met the conditions Labour has set out.
'Labour continues to oppose this divisive policy and calls on the Green Party to do the right thing and rescind it.'
Labour leader Andy Burnham had already ruled out any coalition with the Greens on a national level in future while the policy declaring Zionism a form of racism is in place.
The Prime Minister last month said he condemned it 'unequivocally' and would not support a 'partnership' with the Greens while they keep the motion.
Mr Polanski has said he would not try to overturn the policy, passed by party members, but did want to amend it 'at the first available opportunity'.
Mr Polanski's poll rating has slumped to his worst as Green leader amid the row.
A storm of criticism has seen the motion described as an 'attack' on the Jewish community and the Greens branded 'an extremist party'.
Opponents also claim the motion effectively calls for the eradication of Israel as it refers only to a single Palestinian state.
Mr Polanski controversially skipped the conference vote on the motion on 4 October in order to campaign ahead of last week's Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
His decision to focus on his bid to become an MP rather than remain in Brighton for the conference saw him accused of a 'lack of leadership' by critics from within his own party.
Mr Polanski then went on to lose the contest in the north London constituency to Labour, which added to questions over his leadership of the Greens.
In response to Labour's announcement on Monday, Mr Polanski posted on X: 'This will backfire on Labour.
'The Green Party want to tax billionaires, tackle the climate crisis and stop arming a genocide.
'Labour want to interrupt your local services & impose genocide support from its local councils. Andy Burnham revealing himself and his project...'
The Greens said they were 'hugely disappointed in moves designed by national parties to force local council leaders into jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents'.
A joint statement from the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group added: 'Across the country, Green, Labour, Independent and Liberal Democrat councillors have worked together to provide stable local government, protect services and deliver positive change.
'Leaders across these parties are rightly proud of what those partnerships have achieved.
'Those who issued ultimatums that destabilised power sharing agreements have often ignored the judgements of their own local leaders, failed to respect the choices made by local voters, and are disrupting successful partnerships.'
Tory chairman Kevin Hollinrake said: 'We knew long before the despicable 'Zionism is racism' motion that the Green Party had a problem with anti-Semitism.
'So it beggars belief that it took this motion for Labour to pull out of these deals.
'Labour must explain why it took so long to act and why it needed such an outrageous motion to finally draw the line.'
Former Green co-leader Adrian Ramsay on Sunday said he was 'deeply uncomfortable' with the motion and said the question now was how Mr Polanski and the party responded.
He told the BBC: 'I think there's a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.
'One option is to sort of dig in more down this approach, not only in relation to this motion, but I think that there's a risk it brings with it – a quite divisive, a quite internally focused approach to politics.'
Mr Ramsay also called for the party to focus on its 'core values.'

articles.title_orig: Micron Stock Needs Markets to Clear These 3 Hurdles

articles.content_orig:
Micron has already locked in shipments years ahead, co-designed its next chip with NVIDIA, and posted revenue growth that leaves its peers in the dust, yet the stock trades at a fraction of the multiple those peers command. Something has…
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja .
Our 24/7 Wall St. price target for Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU | MU Price Prediction ) is $1,025.96 over the next 12 months. That is 7.76% above the model’s reference price of $952.10. The model rates the stock a buy with high confidence.
Micron has more than 75% of its fiscal 2027 shipments already committed , and it has signed 26 Supply Commitment Agreements that run through 2030.
That visibility explains why our model still sees value after a huge rally. The modest upside comes from mega-cap muting and a sharp one-month decline.
Shares fell 4.51% to $938.87 on Thursday after Samsung’s earnings showed how high the bar sits for memory stocks. Micron is down 10.91% over the past month but up 2.76% over the past week and 229.21% year to date. It sits 24.1% below its 52-week high of $1,254.61 and about 395% above its low of $192.37.
Fiscal Q4 2026 revenue was $54.23 billion , ahead of the $50.97 billion estimate and up 379.3% year over year. Non-GAAP EPS of $33.42 beat the $31.35 estimate. For fiscal Q1 2027, management guided to revenue of $61.5 billion ± $1.5 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $38.15 ± $1.00.
HBM4 is in high-volume shipments, and HBM4E on 1-gamma DRAM is targeting volume production in calendar 2027. Micron is co-designing HBM4E with NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ).
President Manish Bhatia said that AI demand is “making clear that DRAM is the principal constraint versus logic or power to the data center.”
The consensus analyst target sits at $1,561.91, with 9 Strong Buy and 36 Buy ratings . Our 12-month bull case is $1,351.16, a 41.91% gain.
Memory has always been a cyclical business. Capex reached $30.7 billion in fiscal 2026, and new clean rooms are set to come online in late 2028. Management admitted, “We really don’t have line of sight to when supply and demand balance.”
Among the 19 tracked funds, 10 cut positions in the June quarter. The downside scenario is $770.11. On the other side of the ledger, $62.31 billion of fiscal 2026 free cash flow funds the expansion, and most contract pricing includes floor and ceiling bands.
NVIDIA is the largest driver of HBM demand. Its supply obligations hit $279 billion, mostly for memory for Vera Rubin. NVIDIA trades at 43x earnings, compared with Micron at about 5x forward earnings, even though Micron’s margins are higher (we reverse-engineered what the early signs of the biggest tech winners looked like in a free playbook here ).
Seagate ( NASDAQ:STX ) shares the same AI data-storage tailwind and guides to $9.20 in fiscal Q2 2027 EPS.
Compared with these peers, our 24/7 Wall St. price target looks conservative.
Our 24/7 Wall St. price target is $1,025.96, with a buy rating and 90% confidence. Contracted demand through 2030 is what tips the scale.
The case gets stronger if HBM4E launches on schedule in 2027. It weakens if new supply arrives before demand cools. I see Micron’s earnings power as undervalued.
These projections assume Micron keeps executing on HBM and its supply agreements. The 2026 row comes from the 12-month model, while the 2027 to 2030 rows use the slower five-year path. An glut cycle after 2028 is the biggest risk to these numbers.

Vandita Jadeja is a financial publisher with over a decade of experience writing about financial topics, including investment, savings, retirement, insurance and banking. Vandita is a Chartered Accountant who loves to debunk financial concepts for readers.
Her work has appeared on sites that include The Motley Fool, InvestorPlace, and Benzinga. She covers  investing and focuses on stock picks and price prediction for 24/7 Wall St.
When not looking for the next stock investment opportunity, she can be found traveling, reading, chasing sunsets and enjoying her iced latte.
Micron just crushed earnings for the eighth straight quarter, yet the stock sits 15% below where it was a month ago. With a make-or-break December report on the horizon and 75% of fiscal 2027…

articles.title_orig: The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
articles.title_zh: The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
articles.content_orig:
The Orlando Sentinel, the New York Daily News, the New York Times and affiliated newspapers filed federal lawsuits in Manhattan Monday accusing the technology company Brave Software of using high-tech scraping tools to illegally plunder their websites for exclusive news stories to resell to A.I. giants, including Anthropic and Perplexity.
A Manhattan Federal Court complaint, filed by the News and affiliated Tribune Publishing newspapers the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel, says Brave acts as “the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content” and provides a back door circumventing paywalls to its own users as well as prominent generative A.I. companies to help build their businesses.
“Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties,” the lawsuit alleges. “And the third parties are serving as the knowing receivers of that stolen content, which they have used to build their trillion dollar businesses.”
The company sells copies of the publishers’ content to third parties for training their A.I. models and products and informing responses to users, the suit alleges, in addition to making unauthorized copies of copyrighted works through its own browser, providing free access to paywalled content.
The lawsuit says Brave crawled and copied content from more than 30 billion webpages in its index without identifying itself or providing the owners of websites any mechanism to block its crawler, according to the newspapers’ complaint.
In addition to selling stolen stories to other companies, Brave also has a web browser that provides paywalled copyrighted content to its users, according to the suits. Paywalls provide a critical source of revenue to news organizations as they seek to compete in an evolving news environment by producing quality, original content.
The suits add to a growing pile of cases playing out across the country brought by news organizations and various owners of copyrighted content against tech giants alleging the wholesale theft of content used to train A.I. models. The News, The Times and other papers that filed suit Monday are also suing OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging similar conduct.
In one example detailed in the new lawsuit, a user prompted Brave’s A.I. feature known as “Ask Brave” to show them articles published that day in The News. The chatbot provided the titles of 35 articles that appeared in The News that day behind a paywalland asked, “would you like me to pull up the full text of any of these articles? If so, just tell me which one(s) and I’ll fetch the complete version.”
“AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to. Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry,” said Steven Lieberman, an attorney representing The News and its sister papers with Tribune Publishing in the suit.
The suit lists five legal claims, alleging Brave has committed direct, contributory, and vicarious copyright infringement.
In a statement, Frank Pine, the executive editor at Tribune Publishing and MediaNews Group, said the software company had made “a mockery of our intellectual property laws.”
“Brave, purportedly on behalf of its users but also on behalf of other more well-known AI companies, pillages the internet and resells its ill-gotten gains to anyone who will buy,” Pine said. “Then, proudly touting how it protects the privacy – read that as piracy – of its customers, it attempts to delete evidence of its misdeeds under its ‘Zero Data Retention’ policy.”
The News reached out to Brave Software, Inc., for comment. Anthropic and other A.I. companies accused of buying stolen content from Brave are not named as defendants in Monday’s lawsuits.

articles.title_orig: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
articles.title_zh: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
articles.content_orig:
'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.
Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum

articles.title_orig: Karl Bushby ends 28-year journey at mother's house in Hull
articles.title_zh: Karl Bushby ends 28-year journey at mother's house in Hull
articles.content_orig:
A British adventurer has completed a 28-year walking journey around the world, arriving at his childhood home after travelling some 50,000km (31,070 miles) across jungles, frozen seas and international borders.
Karl Bushby, 57, was embraced by his mother, Angela, outside her terraced house in Hull, northern England, on Monday, beneath a banner reading “Welcome Home Son”.
Hundreds of cheering supporters had welcomed him in the city centre before he made the final stretch home.
“Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd. “Is that it, is it done?”
Bushby began what became known as his Goliath Expedition in Punta Arenas, southern Chile, in November 1998, carrying a tent, a few hundred dollars and a cheap plastic camera.
His goal was to reach his home city by an unbroken route, without using motorised transport to advance his journey.
The route took him north through the Americas, across the ice of the Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia, and onwards through Mongolia and China. He later swam across the Caspian Sea before continuing towards Europe.
Along the way, he negotiated the dense jungle of the Darien Gap between Colombia and Panama, was detained after entering Russia, and faced repeated visa and funding problems.
The global financial crisis in 2008 cost him major sponsors, adding to delays that stretched what he had expected to be a 12-year journey into 28 years.
Last month, he finally swam across the English Channel, clearing the last major obstacle before beginning the final walk home.
“They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here,” he said as he arrived in Hull. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation-states, to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.”
A feature-length documentary about his journey is in production, while Bushby plans to begin a speaking tour around England in the coming weeks.

articles.title_orig: China releases timeline for lunar landing on the Moon, targeting "before 2030"
articles.title_zh: China releases timeline for lunar landing on the Moon, targeting "before 2030"
articles.content_orig:
Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years.
At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”
China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.
According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China’s technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface.
Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China’s space station in low-Earth orbit.
NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, a year or so ahead of China. The United States, which has been working on the Space Launch System rocket for 15 years and the Orion spacecraft even longer, has a more established rocket and crew vehicle.
But there are major questions surrounding the development of a lunar lander, for which both SpaceX and Blue Origin have multibillion-dollar development contracts. Depending on how these projects go, a US lunar landing could be delayed to 2030 or even later.
Although it is virtually impossible for outsiders to glean information about technical milestones achieved inside China’s space program, the country is clearly making credible progress toward reaching the Moon. For example, in August 2025, the China Manned Space Agency successfully tested a high-fidelity mock-up of its 26-ton Lanyue lunar lander. The test used giant tethers to simulate lunar gravity as the vehicle fired its main engines and fine-control thrusters to land on a cratered surface and take off from a location near Beijing.
Recently, the Mengzhou spacecraft for the 2027 test atop a Long March 10A rocket arrived at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan, China, where the mission will launch.
US government assessments of the Chinese space program are restricted, but lawmakers are clearly taking the threat seriously. In the last 12 months, the US Congress and White House have given broad latitude to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman to streamline the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon. He has moved swiftly to cancel the Lunar Gateway space station and planned upgrades to the Space Launch System rocket. And just last week, Isaacman announced plans to help Blue Origin develop a lunar lander by finding a way to boost the Orion spacecraft into low-lunar orbit.
“We have the mandate, we have the resources, and the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do,” he said at the time.
For a couple of years, it has been clear that China has made a major commitment to landing astronauts on the Moon, preferably before the United States returns to the lunar surface, to score a major geopolitical win. Beyond this near-term competition, both NASA and China’s space program are building capabilities to establish a long-term presence at the Moon’s South Pole. As part of this second phase of the contest, Isaacman committed NASA to the development of a base on the surface of the Moon over the next decade.

articles.title_zh: Apple’s ‘Ultra’ smart home robot might have to wait until 2028
articles.content_orig:
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn't affect our editorial independence .
While we all wait for Apple’s HomeView smart home hub to ship, we’re reminded that Apple has been working on a larger, robotic version of the same thing for years. A new report from The Information shares some details about the so-called “HomeView Ultra” (which has reportedly been floated but may or may not launch under that name).
According to the report, this larger HomeView would have a roughly 9-inch display, giving it about 65 percent more screen area than the 7-inch display on the HomeView. It would be attached to its base via a robotic arm that somewhat resembles the iMac G4 or the Pixar lamp. It would feature cameras and sensors that make it aware of its environment, so it can do things like follow you around during a FaceTime call, turn on lights when someone enters a room, or even shoo the cat off the table.
Apple published a research paper last year showing an R&D project for a robotic lamp with personality, and it’s enough to make you instantly want one. If the robotic HomeView similarly animates and moves as though it has a soul, it might even justify the estimated $1,000 price tag.
The report claims that the device, code-named J595, will ship later next year at the earliest, or perhaps in 2028. Most telling is that the hardware has apparently been more or less complete for two years , but is waiting on the software to catch up. Also, there has apparently been some debate about which features should be in the 1st-generation device and which should wait for the 2nd-gen model. According to The Information, the autonomous AI features are ambitious and not ready yet, so the release timing is all about balancing the AI development with the first-generation feature set.
Jason has written about technology for more than 25 years - first in the gaming press, then focusing on enthusiast PCs and general technology. He enjoys learning how complicated technology works and explaining it in a way anyone can understand.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic posts $17B quarterly revenue but losses continue in fresh IPO filing
articles.title_zh: Anthropic posts $17B quarterly revenue but losses continue in fresh IPO filing
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.
The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.
Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.
During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.
The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.
As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds , and quarterly reports from Microsoft , Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.
The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows , causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX , but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.
In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.
"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.
The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut .
Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors . The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives.
"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.

articles.title_orig: Thief: The Dark Project Remastered Brings Its Sticky Fingers to PC and Consoles Next Month
articles.title_zh: Thief: The Dark Project Remastered Brings Its Sticky Fingers to PC and Consoles Next Month
articles.content_orig:
Eidos Montreal, in collaboration with Atari and developer Nightdive Studios, has announced a release date for the upcoming remaster of Thief: The Dark Project . The shadowy rob-'em-up will come creeping onto PC and console platforms on December 3. Originally released back in 1998 and developed by Looking Glass Studios, Thief: The Dark Project was among the first in a wave of stealth-related franchises that launched in the wake of Konami's Metal Gear Solid , replacing the ballistic action of the mid-'90s FPS boom with cooler, quieter, and more trepidatious adventuring. Titles such as Thief, Hitman , Syphon Filter , and Tenchu were among the debutantes that (somewhat) attempted to replace shooting with sneaking.
Set within its own fictional take on the Victorian age, players guide trained-from-birth master thief Garrett as he stalks the shadows of the night, looting monarchs and governors and ultimately stumbling upon a clandestine conspiracy, one that will shake the very foundations of the era itself and usher in a whole new age of treachery and metallurgy.
Nightdive's remaster looks to capture the precision and quiet efficiency of the original PC adventure, while offering a 4K, 60 FPS upgrade for its visual elements, an overhauled control scheme, and more modern UI elements, including a new weapon wheel, a level selector, a behind-the-scenes vault, and a custom campaign designer.
A physical edition of Thief: The Dark Project Remastered is also en route from publisher Clear River Games. The "Trapezoid Edition" contains a physical copy of the game on PS5 disc or Nintendo Switch Game Card, Steelbook casing, a remaster diary, and a unique, trapezoid-shaped box. A Steelbook-only edition is also available. Pre-orders are open now from Clear River Games and selected online retailers.
Thief: The Dark Project Remastered launches December 3 on PlayStation, PC, Xbox Series and Nintendo Switch platforms.

articles.title_orig: Why Orban and Vucic Broke With Trump on Election Denial
articles.title_zh: Why Orban and Vucic Broke With Trump on Election Denial
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Adam Smith, a Washington Democrat who has served in the House since 1996, at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 4, 2025.
When the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee was asked by TIME in May about the prospect of impeaching President Donald Trump, he declined to commit, warning that every impeachment he had witnessed during his decades in Congress had left its target politically stronger. Five months later, Rep. Adam Smith of Washington is prepared to take that risk.
With Democrats hoping to reclaim control of the House in Tuesday's midterm elections, Smith says that he now supports impeaching Trump and is inclined to also back proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , making him one of the most senior Democrats to endorse such a course.
"Trump has become beyond dangerous. He is just completely out of control in what he says and how he is governing," Smith told TIME in an interview a week before the election. "I think we have to try, even if it doesn't succeed."
Smith's endorsement is particularly significant because he would be in line to chair the Armed Services Committee if Democrats win the House, putting him at the center of investigations into the Pentagon's handling of the war with Iran, its approach to Ukraine, and military operations in Latin America.
His position comes as Democrats prepare for the possibility of reclaiming congressional power with little agreement over how aggressively to confront the President. Interviews with more than two dozen Democrats reveal a party broadly convinced that Trump has engaged in conduct warranting impeachment, but deeply divided over whether another attempt to remove him would be an effective use of its authority. Trump's two previous impeachments ended in Senate acquittals, and even a Democratic victory this week is unlikely to produce anything approaching the two-thirds majority required for conviction.
Read more: Calls to Impeach Trump Collide With Reluctant Democratic Leadership
Smith, who has served in the House since 1996, noted previously that he was one of the few House members to have sat through three impeachments. "Every single time the person impeached got stronger after they were impeached than before," Smith told TIME in May, arguing that Democrats needed to consider what another impeachment could realistically achieve rather than pursue it simply to demonstrate their willingness to confront Trump. "I want to make sure that if we're going down that road it's going to help defeat Trump and his poisonous ideology," he said at the time.
Since then, he says, Trump's increasingly conciliatory posture toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, his decisions involving American support for Ukraine, and his public rhetoric have convinced him that the President's continued tenure presents an extraordinary danger. "The Ukraine stuff definitely had a profound impact," Smith says. "When I saw how close he was getting to Putin and shutting off support for Ukraine, being more pro-Putin. I mean, that's a big part of it." He also cites Trump's increasingly "unhinged speeches," including remarks about rising gasoline prices amid the war in the Middle East.
Smith’s willingness to embrace impeachment puts him at odds with more cautious Democrats who want the party to prioritize addressing the economic concerns that have dominated the campaign, while establishing an investigative record that might ultimately lead to impeachment. He acknowledges the formidable obstacles to removing Trump but argues that the political environment has changed since the President's first term. "I don't think it will be viewed as negatively or as partisan as in the previous two efforts, just because the public is waking up to the con game that Trump put on," he says now. "The impeachable offenses have been obvious for a long time.”
Other senior House Democrats are less certain that pursuing impeachment would accomplish much, even if they share Smith's assessment of Trump's conduct. Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who led the House managers during Trump's second impeachment trial in 2021, says he has "little doubt that the president has committed multiple impeachable offenses," citing what he describes as unconstitutional military action and abuses of congressional spending authority. But he draws a distinction between establishing grounds for impeachment and deciding whether another trial would be the best use of Congress's time and political capital.
"The question of whether he committed impeachable offenses and whether we are going to pursue impeachment are two different issues," Raskin tells TIME.
Trump was impeached in 2019 over his dealings with Ukraine and again in 2021 over his role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. Both proceedings ended in acquittal, although seven Republican senators voted to convict him in the second trial. While some Democrats regarded those efforts as necessary to establish a historical and constitutional record, another impeachment could consume months of congressional attention, galvanize Trump's supporters, and leave voters questioning what the party had accomplished with its new majority.
Sen. Adam Schiff of California, who led the prosecution during Trump's first impeachment trial, says Democrats should avoid reaching conclusions before knowing the composition of the next Congress and what investigations might uncover. "There's no question he's been engaging in conduct that is very likely impeachable," Schiff told TIME. "The question is, is it viable?"
Schiff disputes the notion that the earlier impeachment efforts strengthened Trump politically, but argues that Democrats should concentrate initially on investigating corruption that has affected Americans' finances. "Our primary focus ought to be on corruption that has raised the cost of living for people," he says.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has similarly declined to commit to impeachment, saying Democrats "haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out." He has indicated that investigations should help determine whether the House pursues that course.
Some Democrats are looking toward members of Trump's Cabinet, particularly Hegseth, as potentially more viable targets, reasoning that Republicans who would never vote to remove the President might be more willing to turn against a defense secretary whose leadership has drawn criticism from within their own party. "There are Republicans who would support impeaching Hegseth who might not support doing it to Trump," Smith says.
The Defense Secretary has faced mounting scrutiny over his handling of the Iran war, the removal of senior military officers, and the Pentagon's relationship with Congress. Some Republicans have publicly expressed frustration with his leadership and the department's failure to provide adequate information about the war's objectives, costs, and duration. A push to impeach him has already taken shape in the Republican-controlled House, although Trump has defended Hegseth, calling him a "great warrior" and dismissing Democratic efforts to remove him.
Raskin says that impeaching a Cabinet secretary would be less likely to consume Congress's agenda or raise the same concerns about overturning the result of a presidential election. "The question of cabinet officers is a little bit easier because it doesn't necessarily consume all of the policy oxygen in Congress," he says.
However, impeaching Hegseth would require a majority in the House, and removing him would still require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Republicans who have criticized his performance have not necessarily indicated any willingness to support impeachment. But the growing unease over the administration's military decisions, particularly the conduct and costs of the war with Iran, could offer Democrats an opening that does not exist with Trump.

articles.title_orig: Rivian Is Doing The Damn Thing
articles.title_zh: Rivian Is Doing The Damn Thing
articles.content_orig:
There's never a guarantee a startup car company will actually make it. Automotive history is littered with companies that never made it more than a few years, and after some of Rivian's early financial troubles, it wasn't out of the question that the Irvine, California-based company could join that group. Well, following the introduction of the R2 , those fears seem to be all but squashed.
Rivian just posted its third-quarter results for 2026, and the compact-crossover-sized R2 helped raise the automaker's deliveries by 46% year-over-year to 19,248 vehicles, according to Car and Driver . That means Rivian is increasing its yearly sales projection to between 67,000 and 70,000 vehicles — up from 65,000 to 70,000. It also just so happened to outsell the larger and more expensive R1S and R1T flagships combined, as well as the EDV delivery van. I should note that Rivian didn't explicitly say how many R2s it sold, though. This news comes even though the only R2 that Rivian currently sells is the most expensive Performance version of the electric SUV, and the idea that Rivian is still "early in the ramp" of R2 production, according to CEO RJ Scaringe, who spoke with Reuters .
Theoretically, things are only going to get better from here, sales-wise, with the only currently available R2 clocking in at $59,485, including destination. Eventually, a $55,485 Premium trim and $46,485 base model will join its ranks , but the only information we've got is "coming late 2026" and "coming spring 2027," respectively. Of course, even the most expensive R2 is a hell of a lot cheaper than the R1S and R1T, which both start well north of $80,000.
And good news keeps coming, because last week, Scaringe said he was "very confident" Rivian would hit an autonomy milestone this year that would unlock a quarter-billion-dollar tranche of investment money from Uber. That's part of an up-to $1.25 billion investment the rideshare company is making in the automaker through 2031, according to Reuters. It includes an initial $300 million and is contingent on several autonomy milestones. However, Rivian hasn't said exactly what those milestones are. Don't worry, though. Scaringe says Rivian is "right on time."
We do know that the partnership between Uber and Rivian targets the 2028 launch of a driverless R2 robotaxi on Uber's network — starting in a handful of cities and then expanding to about 25 over the next year and a half. Clearly, Rivian is aiming its R2 robotaxi directly at the Tesla Cybercab.
It needs to work, too. As Reuters points out, both the R2's success and the Uber partnership are imperative for making Rivian stick as a company. It's doing pretty well right now, don't get me wrong, but it's still burning through cash like the Bouvier Beale family, and it's looking for any way to narrow those losses.
No matter how you slice it, Rivian is truly showing it's a company that has the ability to stick around and be viable. Once R2 production is fully ramped up and the R3 is introduced, who knows where it could end up? All it needs to do is get that pesky cash burn problem under control.

articles.title_orig: Nearly Two Thousand Chinese Businesses Established in Nicaragua Since Free Trade Agreement Took Effect
articles.title_zh: Nearly Two Thousand Chinese Businesses Established in Nicaragua Since Free Trade Agreement Took Effect
articles.content_orig:
COSTA RICA'S LEADING ENGLISH LANGUAGE NEWSPAPER
Nearly 2,000 Chinese businesses have been established in Nicaragua during the first two years of the free trade agreement with China, according to the president of the Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua. Shujin Huang made the statement to official media outlets after an event marking the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen.
He said the association continues to promote additional investment from China, describing Nicaragua as a safe country with a competitive market. The free trade agreement between the two countries entered into force on January 1, 2024. The Banco Central de Nicaragua reported that net foreign direct investment from China reached 29.3 million dollars in 2025.
That figure represented 1.9 percent of the 1,502.5 million dollars in total net foreign direct investment recorded by the country that year. In 2024, any Chinese flows were not reported separately and would have been included in aggregate categories if present at all. Huang said the businesses operate mainly in commerce, with some also active in free-zone maquilas. The relatively low official investment total relative to the number of establishments indicates that most are small-scale operations.
The Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua was founded in May 2024 and was officially registered as a legal organization under Ministerial Agreement 24-2024-OSFL, allowing it to operate in its own name under Nicaraguan law. Its founding event included participation by Chinese Ambassador Chen Xi and Nicaraguan officials including National Assembly President Gustavo Porras, Foreign Minister Denis Moncada and Presidential Adviser Laureano Ortega Murillo.
As part of the commercial expansion, construction of a Chinatown complex advances in Managua near the Rotonda Universitaria. The project, also known as Plaza China or Plaza 101, involves a two-story structure of approximately 8,000 square meters with an investment of about 3 million dollars. It is planned to house around 100 businesses operated by Chinese, other Asian and Nicaraguan owners.
The site currently holds roughly 30 businesses. Administrators have described the work as being in an intermediate phase, including installation of a stone arch more than six meters high carved in a dragon style and brought from China. The complex is intended to concentrate commercial activity, gastronomy and cultural offerings. Huang cited the existing Plaza China as an example of growing Chinese capital presence, noting that more than ten foreign-investment businesses already operate there.
Nicaragua and China restored diplomatic relations in December 2021 after Managua broke ties with Taiwan. The free trade agreement was signed on August 31, 2023. Official Nicaraguan statements have presented the pact and related initiatives as measures to expand trade and investment opportunities. The association’s stated goals include supporting Chinese investors and promoting the policy of one China.
As of now, the association continues to encourage further arrivals of Chinese capital. Construction on the Managua Chinatown project remains under way, with officials and association representatives describing it as a visible marker of the commercial presence that has developed since the trade agreement took effect. The Banco Central de Nicaragua has not published a full country-by-country breakdown beyond the 2025 net total that places China at 29.3 million dollars.

articles.title_orig: Leicestershire Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
articles.title_zh: Leicestershire Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
articles.content_orig:
The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council has announced he is standing down after comments he made about staff redundancies were leaked online.
Dan Harrison announced on Monday that he would be stepping down from the role he has held since May 2025.
He said he had made the decision after taking advice from senior Reform colleagues, and added deputy council leader Kevin Crook had taken over as acting leader.
It comes after Harrison had apologised after being recorded saying 76 council solicitors would be made redundant, branding them "incompetent", before saying "what I want to look at now is the women", in remarks which were then released on social media.
In a statement, Harrison said it had been the "honour of his life" to lead the county council's first Reform administration.
Harrison has said he will remain as a councillor, representing the Ashby-de-la-Zouch division.
The Conservative opposition at County Hall had called for Harrison to resign after his comments about staff were leaked.
In the recording, Harrison said: "There's 76 solicitors will be made redundant.
"We'll buy in the service, because [they are] incompetent. They're not doing a good job.
"What I want to look at now is the women so it is ongoing, I would like it to be at great pace but I can tell you now if we suddenly drove massive redundancies the liberals would walk away."
Earlier on Monday, Harrison had told the BBC he would not be stepping down - but he later said he made his decision after talking to Crook and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray.
He had apologised over the remarks, which were made on Tuesday during a Reform party meeting.
Despite his apology, Harrison had insisted his remarks had been taken out of context.
Harrison said: "I would like to apologise unreservedly to the staff and officers of the county council for any hurt, distress or offence caused by the publication of these comments, which were made during a heated meeting with the expectation of privacy and confidentiality.
"However, I would like to stress that these discussions were just that, and I have not given any instruction or direction to officers in these matters and that there has not been any discussion nor agreement on these issues with officers."
He added: "I unequivocally reject any suggestion that staffing decisions are being taken based on gender.
"The comments made in that meeting were taken completely out of context."
Before Harrison's resignation, the council's 15 Tory councillors had called for an emergency vote to try to remove him from the leader's role.
Group leader of the Conservative group, Deborah Taylor, said: "That was not a decision we took lightly.
"The serious concerns raised over recent days, particularly around the treatment of council employees and the comments contained in leaked recordings, left us feeling that his position had become untenable.
"His resignation brings an end to his leadership, but it does not mean those concerns should simply be forgotten.
"There are still questions that deserve answers, and it is important that the council learns from what has happened."
The Reform group remains the largest party on the authority, and runs it as a minority administration.
In a statement, Jeevun Sandher and Amanda Hack - Labour MPs for Loughborough and North West Leicestershire respectively - said: "Since taking office in 2025, the Reform UK administration has become increasingly embroiled in controversy and scandal, rather than focusing on delivering for the residents of Leicestershire.
"This is far from an isolated incident. Just last week, councillor [Joseph] Boam was found to have breached the council's own code of conduct through his actions against the former monitoring officer, while other Reform councillors have also been forced to apologise to residents over their behaviour. All of this in less than two years.
"Leicestershire residents deserve better."

articles.title_orig: Best places to retire: 10 US cities ranked for affordability, quality of life
articles.title_zh: Best places to retire: 10 US cities ranked for affordability, quality of life
articles.content_orig:
Air pollution spiked to unhealthy levels around the world in 2021, according to a new report.
The report by IQAir , a company that tracks global air quality, found that average annual air pollution in every country — and 97% of cities — exceeded the World Health Organization’s air quality guidelines , which were designed to help governments craft regulations to protect public health.
Not only is Lake Powell's water level plummeting because of drought, its total capacity is shrinking, too
Only 222 cities of the 6,475 analyzed had average air quality that met WHO’s standard. Three territories were found to have met WHO guidelines: the French territory of New Caledonia and the United States territories of Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands.
India, Pakistan and Bangladesh were among the countries with the worst air pollution, exceeding the guidelines by at least 10 times.
The Scandinavian countries, Australia, Canada, Japan and United Kingdom ranked among the best countries for air quality, with average levels that exceeded the guidelines by 1 to 2 times.
In the United States, IQAir found air pollution exceeded WHO guidelines by 2 to 3 times in 2021.
“This report underscores the need for governments around the world to help reduce global air pollution,” Glory Dolphin Hammes, CEO of IQAir North America, told CNN. “(Fine particulate matter) kills far too many people every year and governments need to set more stringent air quality national standards and explore better foreign policies that promote better air quality.”
Above: IQAir analyzed average annual air quality for more than 6,000 cities and categorized them from best air quality, in blue (Meets WHO PM2.5 guildline) to worst, in purple (Exceeds WHO PM2.5 guideline by over 10 times). An interactive map is available from IQAir .
It’s the first major global air quality report based on WHO’s new annual air pollution guidelines , which were updated in September 2021 . The new guidelines halved the acceptable concentration of fine particulate matter — or PM 2.5 — from 10 down to 5 micrograms per cubic meter.
PM 2.5 is the tiniest pollutant yet also among the most dangerous. When inhaled, it travels deep into lung tissue where it can enter the bloodstream. It comes from sources like the burning of fossil fuels, dust storms and wildfires, and has been linked to a number of health threats including asthma , heart disease and other respiratory illnesses.
Allergy season will start much earlier than normal and be far more intense because of climate crisis, study suggests
Millions of people die each year from air quality issues. In 2016, around 4.2 million premature deaths were associated with fine particulate matter, according to WHO. If the 2021 guidelines had been applied that year, WHO found there could have been nearly 3.3 million fewer pollution-related deaths.
IQAir analyzed pollution-monitoring stations in 6,475 cities across 117 countries, regions and territories.
In the US, air pollution spiked in 2021 compared to 2020. Out of the more than 2,400 US cities analyzed, Los Angeles air remained the most polluted, despite seeing a 6% decrease compared to 2020. Atlanta and Minneapolis saw significant increases in pollution, the report showed.
“The (United States’) reliance on fossil fuels, increasing severity of wildfires as well as varying enforcement of the Clean Air Act from administration to administration have all added to U.S. air pollution,” the authors wrote.
Researchers say the main sources of pollution in the US were fossil fuel-powered transportation, energy production and wildfires, which wreak havoc on the country’s most vulnerable and marginalized communities.
“We are heavily dependent on fossil fuels, especially in terms of transportation,” said Hammes, who lives a few miles from Los Angeles. “We can act smartly on this with zero emissions, but we’re still not doing it. And this is having a devastating impact on the air pollution that we’re seeing in major cities.”
Big-box stores could help slash emissions and save millions by putting solar panels on roofs. Why aren't more of them doing it?
Climate change-fueled wildfires played a significant role in reducing air quality in the US in 2021. The authors pointed to a number of fires that led to hazardous air pollution — including the Caldor and Dixie fires in California, as well as the Bootleg Fire in Oregon, which wafted smoke all the way to the East Coast in July.
China — which is among the countries with the worst air pollution — showed improved air quality in 2021. More than half of the Chinese cities analyzed in the report saw lower levels of air pollution compared to the previous year. The capital city of Beijing continued a five-year trend of improved air quality, according to the report, due to a policy-driven drawdown of polluting industries in the city.
The report also found that the Amazon Rainforest , which had acted as the world’s major defender against the climate crisis, emitted more carbon dioxide than it absorbed last year. Deforestation and wildfires have threatened the critical ecosystem, polluted the air and contributed to climate change.
“This is all a part of the formula that will lead to or is leading to global warming.” Hammes said.
The report also unveiled some inequalities: Monitoring stations remain scant in some developing countries in Africa, South America and the Middle East, resulting in a dearth of air quality data in those regions.
“When you don’t have that data, you’re really in the dark,” Hammes said.
Could Russia's war kick-start a renewable-energy revolution? It depends where in the world you look
Hammes noted the African country of Chad was included in the report for the first time, due to an improvement in its monitoring network. IQAir found the country’s air pollution was the second-highest in the world last year, behind Bangladesh.
Tarik Benmarhnia, a climate change epidemiologist at Scripps Institution of Oceanography who has studied the health impact of wildfire smoke, also noted that relying only on monitoring stations can lead to blind spots in these reports.
“I think it is great that they relied on different networks and not only governmental sources,” Benmarhnia, who was not involved in this report, told CNN. “However, many regions do not have enough stations and alternative techniques exist.”
The UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change concluded in its 2021 report that, in addition to slowing the speed of global warming, curbing the use of fossil fuels would have the added benefit of improving air quality and public health.
Hammes said the IQAir report is even more reason for the world to wean off fossil fuel.
“We’ve got the report, we can read it, we can internalize it and really devote ourselves to taking action,” she said. “There needs to be a major move towards renewable energy. We need to take drastic action in order to reverse the tide of global warming; otherwise, the impact and the train that we’re on (would be) irreversible.”
